claims.claim: On September 8, Google DeepMind introduced AlphaGenome Atlas: a research resource where scientists can look up predicted molecular effects of every possible one-letter DNA change in the human genome, instead of calculating each prediction afresh.
The Atlas includes about nine billion such changes.
In a rare epilepsy case, the report’s ranking put an overlooked DNM1 DNA change at the top. The prediction said it could make cells join a gene message differently.
Researchers then tested 265 nearby DNA letters in five kinds of laboratory-grown cells. Twelve variants produced the predicted kind of longer gene message.
The report says Atlas and its ranking score predict molecular effects and are only part of the evidence needed for clinical diagnoses.

sources.passage: We’ve used AlphaGenome to predict the molecular impact of every possible single-letter change in the human genome. All nine billion of them.
sources.additionalPassage: AlphaGenome Atlas is available to researchers around the world, with coding and non-coding variations available.
sources.limitations: Official announcement; it describes the resource and availability, not diagnosis, patient benefit or clinical deployment.

sources.passage: we calculated the difference between reference and alternate allele predictions for all ~9 billion SNVs in hg38 using AlphaGenome.
sources.additionalPassage:
For a proband with epileptic encephalopathy (Fig. 3B), the top ranked variant by AVI was a heterozygous noncoding VUS in intron 10 of DNM1 (chr9:128225994:G>A, HGVS: NM_004408.4:c.1335+1605G>A) affecting a brain-specific transcript isoform encoding for the dynamin protein. Prediction of RNA-seq track coverage of the reference and alternative alleles showed that the variant creates a brain-specific cryptic splice acceptor site resulting in a 13 amino acid (aa) in-frame extension of exon 10a (Fig. 3C).
We then performed high-throughput experiments in which the 265 nucleotides upstream of exon 10a were mutagenized and assayed in a minigene reporter assay across 5 cell lines (40) (fig. S9D, Table S3, Data S1 and Methods)). We identified 12 intronic variants that led to in-frame exon extensions
Atlas and AVI are research tools that predict molecular effects, and therefore can only act as part of the evidence chain leading to clinical diagnoses, and are not sufficient evidence on their own.
sources.limitations: Technical report with research examples and laboratory work. It does not establish a patient-ready diagnostic, treatment improvement, patient benefit, broad clinical deployment or independent replication.

fragments.text: AlphaGenome Atlas lets researchers look up predicted effects of DNA changes.

On September 8, Google DeepMind introduced AlphaGenome Atlas: a research resource where scientists can look up predicted molecular effects of every possible one-letter DNA change in the human genome, instead of calculating each prediction afresh. The Atlas includes about nine billion such changes.

That can speed the first sorting step. A DNA variant is a difference in a DNA sequence. If a study has many variants to investigate, the Atlas can point researchers toward changes that may affect biology, so they can decide what to examine more closely.

One example shows the sequence in real life. In a rare epilepsy case, the report’s ranking put an overlooked DNM1 DNA change at the top. The prediction said it could make cells join a gene message differently. Researchers then tested 265 nearby DNA letters in five kinds of laboratory-grown cells. Twelve variants produced the predicted kind of longer gene message.

That is a research lead followed by one laboratory check—not a personal diagnosis. The report says Atlas and its ranking score predict molecular effects and are only part of the evidence needed for clinical diagnoses. It also calls for evaluation across diverse genetic ancestries.

The news is faster access to a research starting point. It does not replace testing a candidate in the relevant biological setting. When you read a gene-prediction headline, ask: what did it predict, what experiment followed, and what would still need to happen before it could inform someone’s care?
